1.1: 1.1 Argument. Peter shows that the disciples of the unconquered Savior, scattered through the whole world, are pilgrims in this age, and with all solicitude urges them to repent of their past life and advance in a new life: Simon Peter, son of Jonah, of the province of Galilee, from the village of Bethsaida, brother of Andrew the apostle. To the strangers. BEDE. Strangers in Latin, in Greek proselytes, etc., down to having: Beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims. Of the dispersion. In the year of the ascension Stephen died, and many were scattered by fear. Of Pontus. All these provinces of the Greeks are in Asia, but there is another Bithynia in Europe: from which those who are in Asia, the Bithynians, had their origin. But that which is in Asia, Bithynia, is called greater Phrygia, which is separated from Galatia by the river Hiera.
1.2: 1.2 Grace. Without the grace of Christ, one never comes to the peace of his reconciliation, we can have nothing peaceful except through his grace. And may peace be multiplied. That is, let no adversity draw you back from the praises of God, let every tribulation invite you to praise, because all things are multiplied to happiness: that what you have well begun you may perfectly complete.
1.3: 1.3 He has begotten again. BEDE. When by our merits we had been begotten to death, etc., down to that through cleanness you may be heaven and the seat of God.
1.4: 1.4 Incorruptible. By nature the soul is not incorruptible, but by the grace of God through faith and righteousness it is made incorruptible to the understanding. In you. He who gave you believing power to become children of God has placed in you that perseverance by which you may receive the inheritance in heaven, because he who does not keep the discipline of the Father does not merit his inheritance.
1.5: 1.5 By the power. No one can be kept in goods by the power of his own freedom unless he perfects it from whom you have the beginning of good action. Labor from faith by faith, about to come to eternal salvation, which even if it does not now appear, is nevertheless ready to be revealed, if we are ready.
1.6: 1.6 Now, if it is necessary. If, that is although it be necessary. Or, if it be necessary to be sad, let us not fail.
1.7: 1.7 That the proof, etc., unto praise. When the judge, praising your faith, will say: And you gave me to eat, etc., Matthew 25. More precious than gold. BEDE. The patience of the saints is compared to gold, etc., down to hence he also adds: May be found, etc. Unto praise. That you may be praiseworthy and glorious through constancy in the revelation, that is on the day of judgment, when it will be revealed how great is the power of God. And honor, that it may be said to you: Come, blessed of my Father, Matthew 25.
1.9: 1.9 The salvation of souls. This salvation is much to be loved, because they inquired much about this salvation, when or in what order eternal salvation would come to the world; hence it is said: Many prophets and kings wished to see what you see, and did not see, Matthew 13.
1.10: 1.10 Prophesied. By speaking openly to men and expounding what they themselves had known in the secret of inner contemplation.
1.11: 1.11 Into what or, etc. What time, that is in what year, or under what prince. What kind, warlike or peaceful, or in what order, through the birth of a virgin, or in what other way. The Spirit of Christ. He calls archangels and those near spirits, through whom the Lord works, because they are subject to Christ. Later glories. There are two glorifications of the Lord according to the form of the man he assumed. One by which he rose from the dead, and the other by which he ascended into heaven before the eyes of the apostles. A third remains, and it will be in the sight of men, when he comes in majesty to render to each according to his works.
1.12: 1.12 But to you they ministered. He says this to admonish them to take care of the salvation offered, which earlier saints so loved. By the Holy Spirit. BEDE. The Spirit in the prophets, the Spirit in the apostles, so it appears that the prophets and apostles announce the same salvation. They announce it as coming, these as fulfilled. There is therefore one Church, a part of which preceded the coming of Christ and a part follows.
1.13: 1.13 Wherefore. Because so great grace has been promised you, that you may see revealed that which now the angels see, take care to be so much the more worthy to be able to receive it. Hope. Wait securely in mind, and chaste in body. For he who does not know how to please the Lord, rightly lacking hope of goods, fears lest it come the sooner.
1.14: 1.14 Children. And that you may be able to wait securely, be children obedient to a Father who corrects.
1.15: 1.15 Holy. That is sanctified and sanctifying you that in all conduct you may be holy: hence: Be you also perfect, etc.
1.17: 1.17 In fear, etc. JEROME. I, defiled with all the filth of sins, by days and nights am busied with trembling to pay the last farthing. And the time when it will be said to me, Jerome, come forth. Of your sojourning. That you may be able to be holy, have your conduct in fear, in the time of your sojourning as long as you are in the exile of this world. Blessed is he who is always fearful, I say this if you invoke God, as if to say: You do not truly invoke God unless you are anxious and fearful.
1.19: 1.19 But with the precious blood. The order of the letter is: but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb unspotted and undefiled. Here he touches Levitical and priestly celebrations. But he signifies a soul made clean by righteousness which is offered to God.
2.1: 2.1 Laying aside therefore all malice. What is malice? unless the love of hurting? What is guile? unless to do one thing and pretend another? What is flattery? unless seduction by false praise? What is envy? unless hatred of another's happiness? What is detraction? unless a reproof more biting than true? Malice delights in another's evil. Guile doubles the heart. Flattery the tongue. Detraction wounds reputation.
2.2: 2.2 As newborn. BEDE. Because you are so reborn, and made eternal children, be such by zeal of good conduct, as infants recently born are by nature of age. Rational. Be infants by malice removed, yet rational by wisdom: and let no reason draw you to the crafty ways of the world, but be without guile; hence: Be prudent as serpents, Matthew 10, etc. Desire milk. BEDE. He touches those who come disdainful to hear sacred readings, ignorant of that thirst and hunger of which the Lord says: Blessed are they who hunger and thirst for righteousness, Matthew 5. And therefore they come more slowly to the perfect increases of salvation, so that they can be refreshed with solid food of the word, that is, know the divine secrets, or do greater goods. That you may grow in it. That by learning well, through the sacred things of the Lord's incarnation you may come to the contemplation of the divine majesty.
2.3: 2.3 If indeed you have tasted. THE SAME. On this condition, the malice of the heart being purged, desire the life-giving nourishment of Christ, if you savor how great the divine sweetness is. For he who tastes nothing of his sweetness, it is no wonder if he does not avoid defiling himself with earthly desires.
2.5: 2.5 As living stones. Through unbelief indeed hard and without feeling, but through discretion instructed they are made alive and fit to be joined by charity in the building of God. Be built. To offer good works, alms, prayers and yourselves. Through Jesus Christ. This refers to all: be built, you are priests, you offer, and all this through Jesus Christ, by whose grace you have all things.
2.6: 2.6 Wherefore, to confirm that the Lord, on account of his firmness, is rightly called a stone, etc.
2.7: 2.7 To you therefore who believe is honor, to those who do not believe, etc., which the builders rejected. So rejected by these as by those, and that stone here, that is to believers, is made the head of the corner, and to unbelievers is made a stone of offense and a rock of scandal.
2.8: 2.8 And a stone of offense. Since Christ is the stone on which the good are supported and rest secure, to unbelievers he will be a cause of offense in the present, to those not believing in him, and therefore they fall from vice to vice. In the future he is a rock of scandal, because against that stone Christ, whom they trampled as lowly, their steps will be dashed, and they will fall into the eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels. They stumble at the word. He stumbles at the word who, because he has heard the word; he stumbles in mind when he does not believe what he heard, whose folly he increases. Nor do they believe in whom they were placed: by nature men were made for this, to believe God and obey his will.
2.9: 2.9 But you a chosen race. This testimony of praise once given to the ancient people through Moses the Apostle gives to the Gentiles who believe in Christ: who like a cornerstone united the Gentiles into that salvation which Israel had in itself. A royal priesthood. United to the body of the High Priest, who ought to hope for the kingdom and to offer to God victims of an immaculate conduct. Of acquisition, in the blood of his redemption as the people of Israel was once redeemed from Egypt by the blood of the lamb. Hence also in the following verse he mystically recalls the old history, and teaches that this was specially fulfilled in one people. That you may announce. BEDE. As those freed from Egypt sang a triumphal song to the Lord, so we, after the darkness is dispelled, after receiving remission through Christ who leads us to the homeland of heavenly brightness, ought to render to God thanks worthy of heavenly benefits.
2.10: 2.10 Who once. THE SAME. From this it is proved that he writes this epistle to those who from the Gentiles had come to the faith. These verses are taken from the prophecy of Hosea in which the calling of the Gentiles is treated.
2.11: 2.11 Beloved. THE SAME. So far he has instructed the Church in general, etc., down to the liberties of a more relaxed life to bear the greater dangers of tickling allurements. As strangers. The less set your mind on earthly things, the more you remember that you have a homeland in heaven. The reprobate have here a homeland, for whose desires they long, therefore they will be banished into perpetual exile, lacking pleasures.
2.12: 2.12 Considering from good works. THE SAME. It has most often happened that pagans who blamed the faith of the Christians, afterward considering their good conduct, began to praise Christ.
2.13: 2.13 Be subject therefore to every human creature for God's sake, whether to the king, etc. And that your conduct may please all, do not resist any dignity of men, any person, any rule to which God has willed you to be subject, because there is no power but from God, and he who resists the power resists the ordinance of God. And he explains creature by parts saying, whether to the King, etc.
2.14: 2.14 As sent by him. Many times God permits some evil man to exercise tyranny, that the wicked may be confounded and the good the more approved. For vengeance. BEDE. He says this, not that it always so happens, but he simply relates what the action of a ruler ought to be, who even if he condemns the good, what he does is no less to their praise, if the good patiently bear his wickedness and wisely resist his craftiness.
2.15: 2.15 But the praise of the good. Because it is so. The truly devout, whatever the rulers do, obtain praise: because God wills this, who uses even the wicked for good, wherefore you also use even them for good, whether they are good or bad, making the ignorance of imprudent men silent. That in whatever way you may use them for good, and through them merit praise, and they themselves not find what to blame in you, while you even honor and bear with them, though they are unclean.
2.16: 2.16 Not as a cloak. BEDE. Not having your liberty as a cloak of malice, etc., down to hence he adds: But as servants of God.
2.17: 2.17 Love the brotherhood. THE SAME. And among all, even those who by temporal condition are subject to you, love as brothers in Christ.
2.18: 2.18 Servants be subject. So far he has exhorted free men to subjection, now he speaks to servants, that they too be subject to masters. Not only to the good. Another translation: Not only to the good and modest: but also to the more difficult. Froward. That is undisciplined. Schola in Greek, in Latin a place, where they came together to hear masters of the liberal arts, hence schola is interpreted leisure, because there they had leisure for studies. Scholastics therefore are the learned. The froward are the unlearned and rustic. See how above he warned to submit to human creature for God's sake.
2.19: 2.19 For if for conscience toward God. If for God who knows the good intention someone patiently suffering is unjustly beaten by the Lord, when he serves him well, and endures, that is counts light sorrows, this is grace, and by this he is made pleasing to God, and the grace of faith requires this. Suffering unjustly. If you suffer unjustly, you acquire the grace of God. For if you bear patiently the punishments inflicted by masters, I say you sinning by not wishing to obey them and buffeted by the masters themselves, that is often corrected by them, that through buffets you may be brought to obey, what grace will that be to you? None, you will receive nothing from God for this.
2.21: 2.21 For to this you were called. He greatly glorifies the condition of servants, whom, doing good and beaten without fault by cruel and wicked masters, he affirms to be imitators of the Lord's passion. Because Christ also. BEDE. Whereas above he instructed servants specially, now he instructs the whole Church that he may also recall to masters what their author endured for their salvation or deliverance.
2.23: 2.23 But he delivered himself to him who judged unjustly. To those judging according to an unjust law, as he being just. Or, he delivered to God the Father those who judged unjustly, that is those who most wickedly condemned him and pressed for his death, that by taking punishments they might be instructed. He touches the evangelical parable, where it is said that the pious shepherd, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the desert, came to visit the one that had perished.
2.25: 2.25 And bishop. Or visitor, which is the same. For a bishop is an overseer, because the eyes of the Lord are upon the just, and his ears are open to their prayers. And, The Dayspring from on high has visited us.
3.3: 3.3 Whose let it not be. The order of the words is this: whose adornment let it not be braiding of hair, or gold put around, or clothing of garments, that is, let them not be festive garments with which they are clothed. But let your adornment be the hidden man of the heart known to God alone, in the incorruptibility of spirit: spirit, I say, quiet from the assault of vices and modest, that it not be proud, which spirit, though not evident to men, yet is rich in the sight of God.
3.7: 3.7 Husbands. As if to say: as I commanded wives that by their holy conduct they gain their husbands and serve them, likewise I command you, O husbands, that by your conduct wives be gained, and keep them, I say with them, rendering the debt, dwelling together. And this according to conscience, not in passions of desire, but as we understand God wills, namely that you beget children for the worship of one God, I say giving honor to the weaker female vessel, both in clothing and in providing other necessaries for them: and if at times it pleases them to abstain from intercourse, give honor, because they are weaker. Give also as to co-heirs of the grace now given by God, and of the life to be given in the future, or of the life to be given for grace.
3.9: 3.9 Not rendering. Not only cease to render evil for evil, but also for cursing give blessing. Because in this. BEDE. Because he had forbidden to render evil for evil, etc., down to we also will receive a crown for their salvation (which we prayed for). That you may inherit a blessing. The judge saying: Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom, Matthew 25. Or the blessing is understood by which the saints in the future life will bless God. What each wishes to come to in the future, let him strive to meditate and do in the present, let him bless the Maker and his brother, and render himself worthy of brotherly blessing.
3.13: 3.13 And who is. BEDE. Therefore you ought to turn from evil and do good, because no one can draw you back from good, nor from the crown, if you wish to persist, indeed they profit while they wish to harm.
3.14: 3.14 But the fear. In the future you will be blessed, but in the present do not fear their fear, that is those things which in them can seem fearful, such as royal power, and the like.
3.15: 3.15 But the Lord. The holiness of Christ; how great it is of incomprehensible glory, look at with inmost affection of heart, and so sanctify Christ himself in you, that he depart neither from memory nor from love. He who does not consider this holiness falls to the snares of the enemy. To everyone who asks. To one wishing to receive on loan reasonable sums, let us not refuse. Hence Paul: Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, knowing how you ought to answer each. For those outside, that is not yet faithful, wish to know something about the hope that is in you. He therefore who presides over ecclesiastical teaching should instruct the patient and stop the rebellious.
3.16: 3.16 But with modesty. In the very knowledge of teaching he warns that the quality of teaching be observed, that humility be shown both in living and in speaking.
3.17: 3.17 It is better. BEDE. So you ought to suffer slanderers and confound them, etc., down to is removed and prepared for eternal vengeance.
3.18: 3.18 He might offer to God. THE SAME. Because even then if any wished to believe the preaching of the Lord (which they set before through the life of the faithful), he rejoiced to offer them to God the Father. But if any spoke against the good as against evildoers, they were confounded when the flood was imminent.
3.19: 3.19 In prison. THE SAME. Those who have their sense darkened by darkness are rightly said even in this life to be shut up in prison, and in this inner prison of the mind are weighed down by unjust works, until, freed from the flesh, they are cast into the outer darkness of eternal damnation. The just also have a prison here, but of tribulations, the reprobate of vices.
3.20: 3.20 When they awaited the patience of God. When the patience of God invited them to repentance, sparing them for a hundred years in which Noah was building the ark, by which was shown what would be in the world. They themselves therefore did not use the patience of God for repentance, but awaited it as though it would last forever. Noah. Noah is interpreted rest, and signifies Christ who gives his faithful rest of souls. While the ark was being built. BEDE. As the ark was built of smoothed wood, so the Church of the gathering of faithful souls: and as when the world perished few were saved through water: so in comparison with those who perish the number of the elect is small, because narrow is the way that leads to life, and few are they who find it.
3.21: 3.21 Which also now saves you, the like form. Baptism saves, baptism I say of like form, that is made like in all things to that ark, because whatever was done there carnally is done here spiritually. Not the putting away, etc. I do not say that baptism saves where there is only the putting away of the filth of the flesh, that is where the flesh is only washed outwardly (which heretics had), but where there is the interrogation of a clean conscience, that is, where a good conscience of the one to be baptized is asked and required by the baptizer: because such baptism saves, another kills; the interrogation is made tending toward God, that through a good conscience one may be made one with God.
3.22: 3.22 Swallowing up death. BEDE. What we swallow, we do that in our bodies the thing taken may nowhere appear: the Lord so wholly consumed death that nothing against him prevailed, and, the appearance of a true body remaining, the stain of former frailty was absent. This is promised to us also, hence he adds, that we also might be made heirs of eternal life. The angels subject to him. We do not doubt that the angels were always subject to the Son of God, but here he mentions subjection to show that the humanity assumed was so raised in the resurrection that it is preferred to every power of angelic dignity. Hence, You have subjected all things under his feet, Psalm 8.
4.1: 4.1 Because he who suffered. BEDE. He who by fear of heavenly judgments extinguishes carnal desires in the mind is already like Christ crucified, as dead to sins. He lives only for the service of God.
4.4: 4.4 Blaspheming. THE SAME. Even if they blaspheme you for being set apart from their unbelief, yet seeing in your conduct works of righteousness and piety they marvel, and in a way revere the faith.
4.6: 4.6 For for this reason the gospel was preached also to the dead. BEDE. So great is God's care that we be mortified in the flesh, etc., down to that their reason may condemn the evils in the wicked.
4.7: 4.7 Of all. Because he had said that the living and the dead are to be judged in judgment, lest anyone flatter himself over the distance of the future judgment, he wisely warns that though the coming of the last crisis is uncertain, yet it is certain to all that in this life we cannot long continue. Watch in prayers. BEDE. That the mind think nothing but only what it prays. When we stand to pray, let every carnal thought withdraw, let the sincere intention of the heart pray to God not by the sound of the voice but by the sense of the mind.
4.8: 4.8 Having continual charity. THE SAME. He who through charity admonishes, rebukes his neighbor, etc., down to although it cannot always be shown publicly.
4.11: 4.11 If any man speaks. If anyone has knowledge of speaking, let him impute it not to himself but to God: let him fear lest, beyond the will of God, or the authority of the holy Scriptures, or beyond usefulness, he teach his brother, or be silent about what is to be said. If any man ministers. BEDE. When you have done all things well and according to his will, attribute them not to your merits but to his grace, that others seeing your good works may glorify your Father who is in heaven.
4.12: 4.12 Beloved, do not. If you suffer the heat of tribulations which are inflicted against reason for your proof and glory, do not therefore think you are exiles from the members of Christ, and do not marvel at the evils inflicted, that through them God may try and prove you, because it is ancient and frequent that the elect of God suffer adversity in the present for eternal salvation.
4.14: 4.14 You will be blessed, etc. He who suffers for the name of Christ is blessed; for you ought not to believe that you suffer without reward, as those who suffer for their crimes and are punished unwillingly. His Spirit rests upon you. Because they will rest upon you who suffer, both in the present in part for doing well, and in the future perfectly for rewarding.
4.17: 4.17 For the time, etc. BEDE. Therefore one must suffer for the name of Christ, etc., down to but the reprobate now spend their days in their goods, and in a moment will go down to hell, Job 21.
4.18: 4.18 And if the just man, etc. THE SAME. This is taken from Proverbs according to the old edition. In ours, which follows the Hebrew truth, it is thus: If the just man receives on earth, how much more the wicked and sinner? that is, if so great is the frailty of mortal life that not even the just (who are to be crowned in heaven) pass through it without tribulations on account of the innumerable stain of vitiated nature: how much more those who are deprived of heavenly glory look to the sure destruction of their perpetual damnation! AUGUSTINE. You ask the cause why the just man can scarcely be saved in the judgment of God, and why? unless because it is certain that the justice of God is so great that sometimes what seems just in men by our judgment is found unjust by the judgment of God, according to that: Man sees the face, but God looks at the heart, I Kings 16. BEDE. It is not laborious for God to deliver the just man; but that it may be shown that the whole human nature was deservedly condemned, God himself is not willing to deliver easily from so great an evil: for which reason also sins are easy and righteousness laborious, except to those who love: but charity, which makes men loving, is from God.
4.19: 4.19 Let them commit their souls, etc. And because judgment begins at the house of the Lord, and through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God, this remains for those who are to suffer: that when they suffer according to what God wills, that is, for righteousness' sake, they commit their souls to God, presuming nothing of themselves, so that he may purge them here as he wills, and in the future make them blessed, because he is faithful in rendering good to those whom he created. I say they suffer in doing good, not for sins.
5.1: 5.1 The elders. Having earlier warned free men and servants, husbands and wives themselves, distinctly, after a common exhortation interposed, he thus addresses the old and the young.
5.2: 5.2 Not by constraint. Do not preach the Gospel in order to be able to live off the Gospel, but willingly according to God, that is, only with a view to the heavenly reward.
5.5: 5.5 Likewise, young men. BEDE. After he had taught how the elders should preside, etc., down to he then adds, admonishing in general: And all of you, show humility to one another, the old by teaching, the young by following.
5.6: 5.6 Be humbled. BEDE. What the grace is that God confers on the humble, etc., down to a fitting reward of exaltation follows.
5.8: 5.8 As a roaring lion, etc. As the roaring of a lion blocks the ears so that they take in no other sound, so the devil, by terrifying the minds of the faithful and suggesting unlawful things, turns them from the way of truth so that they do not hear the voice of Christ.
5.9: 5.9 Knowing. BEDE. Have so much the greater confidence, etc., down to be ashamed that you alone, beyond all others, cannot suffer.
5.12: 5.12 I have written. To you, he says, I have written, not commanding but beseeching, and testifying by the authority of the Scriptures that this is the true grace which I proclaim in writing, because there is salvation in no other, in whom you must be saved. Or, beseeching you to make this grace in which you stand, and with which you have been imbued, truly your own grace, and to hold it as profitable to you. He who scorns grace does not diminish grace, but renders it not his own, that is, not useful to himself.
5.13: 5.13 In Babylon. BEDE. He calls Rome Babylon because of the confusion of manifold idolatry, etc., down to cannot be immune from the pressure of the devil.
